**Where we are ahead:** nothing yet. **Where we are behind:** a full (EC)DHE handshake with a
certificate works against OpenSSL 3.5's `s_client`, Go 1.26's crypto/tls client, the
collection's `tlsclient` and Zig std's client, sans-I/O or through the
blocking `Connection`, with its certificate and key loaded from openssl's PEM forms;
BoringSSL's BoGo suite passes 339 tests with none failing (`tools/bogo/passing.txt`; everything
else is unimplemented or disabled with a reason). HelloRetryRequest (M2 step 1), KeyUpdate
both ways (step 2), session tickets with resumption (step 3), client certificates (step 4) and
OCSP / SCT stapling (step 5) work. **rustls parity (step 6):** of the 436 BoGo server tests
at TLS 1.3 that rustls 0.23.43 passes (`tools/bogo/rustls-owed.txt`), 247 pass here, 140 are
disabled with a reason (121 run at TLS 1.2 under a name without a version; 19 deliberate
divergences: P-521 and ML-DSA client keys, four with rustls's own behaviour that the pinned
runner cannot map, extensions this server ignores), and 49 are gaps: 0-RTT (27),
certificate compression (6), P-521 and ML-DSA server keys (12), standalone ML-KEM-1024 (4) — see
*Backlog*. SCT stapling
(RFC 6962) is beyond rustls, which dropped it; BoringSSL and OpenSSL have it.
**tlsfuzzer (M2 exit gate, 2026-10-21):** 50 of its TLS 1.3 scripts run
(`interop-tlsserver -- --tlsfuzzer DIR`, counts in `tools/tlsfuzzer/baseline.tsv`); against
the 17 scripts qap's fork of ianic/tls.zig is held to, none is worse except two deliberate
divergences (`connection-abort`: no tickets for a client without `psk_key_exchange_modes`;
`obsolete-curves`: JDK 11 compatibility), three are better (`signature-algorithms` 278/4
over all its cases, `ecdsa-support` with a P-384 key, `eddsa` with an Ed25519 key), and
`legacy-version` reached the fork's 10/0 with a fix found by it.

## What this module is, and what it is not

A TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) server for the collection, built as a buffer-driven (sans-I/O) core with
a blocking wrapper on top, on the `tls13` handshake building blocks (key schedule,
CertificateVerify, key exchange, transcript) and the collection's AEADs (`aesgcm`,
`chachapoly`). It is being built to replace qap's fork of a third-party TLS server, milestone by
milestone (plan: `~/CML/tlsserver-2026-10-20/DESIGN.md`).

**Today:** `Server`, a sans-I/O full handshake — ClientHello → ServerHello, compatibility CCS,
EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished → the client's Finished — then
application data both ways and close_notify, over the record layer (header, in-place protection,
the receive side, alerts), the ClientHello decoder and the message encoders. It handshakes with
OpenSSL 3.5's `s_client` (ECDSA P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, RSA-PSS and ML-DSA-65
certificates; all three suites; X25519MLKEM768, X25519, secp256r1, secp384r1, ML-KEM-1024;
ALPN; with and without SNI), with Go's
crypto/tls client (the same, Go's own defaults), with `tlsclient` and with Zig std's client;
`Connection` drives it over a `std.Io.Reader`/`Writer` pair; `keys.CertKeyPair` loads the
certificate chain and private key from PEM. A client that sent no share for the chosen group
gets a HelloRetryRequest. After the handshake KeyUpdate works both ways: a client's turns the
receive key over (and `update_requested` is answered once), the server rekeys on its own at
`max_records_per_key` (2^23 records, asking the client to rekey too) or when the application
calls `keyUpdate`; at most `max_key_updates` (32) KeyUpdates may come between two
application-data records (rustls, BoringSSL). With `Config.tickets` it issues NewSessionTickets
and resumes them (below). With `Config.client_auth` it asks for a client certificate, verifies
the chain (`ClientCertVerifier`; `X509Verifier` = `x509.verifyChain` with clientAuth) and the
client's CertificateVerify, and reports the leaf (`peerCertificate`), resumptions included. It
is not yet the server qap runs (M3: qap's seams and performance).

**Never in scope:** TLS 1.2 and earlier, and DTLS (the `dtls` module). **Not in v1:** 0-RTT
early data, kTLS, ECH and post-handshake client authentication (*What is deliberately not
done*).

## Wire format / algorithm

### Certificate and key loading (`keys.zig`)

`CertKeyPair.fromPem(out, gpa, chain_pem, key_pem)`: every `CERTIFICATE` block of `chain_pem`
(leaf first; blocks of other labels skipped, so one combined file can serve as both arguments,
and a file concatenated without a final newline still splits), and the first private-key block
of `key_pem`:

| Label | Content | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| `EC PRIVATE KEY` | RFC 5915 ECPrivateKey; the `[0]` curve required | P-256, P-384 |
| `PRIVATE KEY` | RFC 5958 PrivateKeyInfo / OneAsymmetricKey (v0 or v1) | EC P-256/P-384/P-521 (a `[0]` inside must agree), Ed25519 (RFC 8410: no parameters, a 32-octet seed), RSA (`rsa.fromPkcs8`), ML-DSA-44/65/87 (RFC 9881: no parameters; the `seed` and `both` forms — `both` must match its seed; `expandedKey` alone is `UnsupportedKey`, as only its public half could be checked against the leaf) |
| `RSA PRIVATE KEY` | PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey | RSA (`rsa.SecretKey.fromDer`: two-prime, consistency-checked) |
| `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY`, or any key with RFC 1421 `Proc-Type` headers | — | refused, `UnsupportedKey` |

An EC scalar shorter than the order is left-padded (as OpenSSL reads it); longer, zero or ≥ the
order is `MalformedKey` (std's `SecretKey.fromBytes` checks nothing, so the range is checked
here). Every chain entry must be readable by `x509.spkiOf`, not merely DER
(`MalformedCertificate`); an END line must name its BEGIN's label (`InvalidPem`); CRLF is
accepted. An RSA key under an id-RSASSA-PSS leaf is `UnsupportedKey`. Other curves (P-521, secp256k1) and algorithms are `UnsupportedKey`.
The key must belong to the leaf (`x509.spkiOf`: algorithm, named curve, and the public key
derived from the private one equal to the certificate's), else `KeyMismatch` — rustls's
`keys_match`, Go's `X509KeyPair`. DER is read strictly: definite lengths, minimal length
octets, at most two length octets. `certifiedKey()` borrows from the pair (it must not move);
`deinit` wipes the key and frees.

**The handshake** (`server.Server`, RFC 8446 §2 Figure 1, full handshake): the caller feeds
received octets (`feed` → `need_more`, `handshake_done`, `app_data`, `peer_closed`, and how much
was consumed) and drains `pendingOutput`. On the ClientHello, in rustls 0.23's order and with its
alerts: compression must include null (`illegal_parameter`); an invalid SNI is
`illegal_parameter`; no `signature_algorithms` is `handshake_failure`; no TLS 1.3 in
`supported_versions` is `protocol_version`; the certificate is fixed or chosen by
`CertificateSelector` from the SNI (`access_denied` when none); the signature scheme is the key's
first candidate the client offers (or, with `CertifiedKey.signature_schemes`, the first of
those the key can make and the client offers); the suite is the client's first enabled one; the
group is the client's first `supported_groups` entry the server enables (with
`Config.server_order`, suite and group go by the server's lists instead, BoringSSL
`SSL_OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE`) — every one of these without a match
is `handshake_failure`; compression other than exactly null is `illegal_parameter`; no
`key_share` is `handshake_failure`, two shares of one group or a share that does not exchange
(`kex`: wrong length, low order) `illegal_parameter`, no share for the chosen group
gets a HelloRetryRequest (below); `pre_shared_key` without `psk_key_exchange_modes` is
`missing_extension` (otherwise, without `Config.tickets`, the offer is ignored: full handshake;
with it, see *Resumption*); ALPN is the server's first
protocol the client offers (`no_application_protocol` when the server has some and none match).
The server then sends ServerHello (plaintext), a compatibility CCS, and under its handshake key
EncryptedExtensions (the ALPN choice; an empty `server_name` acknowledging a DNS-name SNI),
Certificate (on the leaf, an OCSP staple if the client sent `status_request` of type ocsp and
an SCT list if it sent `signed_certificate_timestamp`, each when configured and non-empty),
CertificateVerify and
Finished, one record per message; it switches its sending key to the application secret and
waits for the client's Finished (`decrypt_error` if it does not verify), after which application
data flows. Early data is never accepted; records the client sent under a 0-RTT key are skipped
(up to 2^14 octets). Every refusal queues its alert in `pendingOutput` (sealed once the server
sends protected) and leaves the connection dead (`error.Closed` afterwards); every key and secret
is wiped at that moment. `close` queues close_notify and keeps reading.

**Resumption** (RFC 8446 §2.2, §4.2.11, §4.6.1; rustls 0.23 rules, `Config.tickets`). After
the client's Finished the server sends `Tickets.count` (2) NewSessionTickets packed into one
record — none when the client did not offer `psk_dhe_ke`, the only mode served (no `psk_ke`).
Each ticket is a `Ticketer` blob (`StekTicketer`: `tlsresume`'s AES-256-GCM STEK ring, key id
as AAD, keys past the rotation policy's lifetime refused) over `tlsresume.select.SessionState`
(resumption master secret over the transcript through the client's Finished, a one-octet nonce
= the ticket's index, issue time, `ticket_age_add`) followed by this server's `TicketFields`:
format 2, SNI, ALPN, the client's certificate (DER leaf, ≤ 4096 octets; empty without one) and
the scheme it signed with, suite — the suite last, read from the end, so a SHA-384 ticket opened
with a SHA-256 prefix can never match the negotiated suite. `ticket_lifetime` is
`min(Tickets.lifetime_s, 7 days)` (12 h by default, rustls), and each ticket carries an empty
GREASE extension (RFC 8701 §3.2, as BoringSSL). A ticket that cannot be sealed or has no room
in the output is not sent, nor are the rest. On a ClientHello with `pre_shared_key` (the second
one after a HelloRetryRequest; the first is not looked at), `tlsresume.select.selectPsk`
takes the first of up to 32 identities that opens, is younger than 7 days and the configured
lifetime, has the negotiated suite and the same SNI (rustls `can_resume`; the client's reported
age is not checked — it matters only for early data); that identity's binder over
`Truncate(ClientHello)` (after `message_hash` and the HelloRetryRequest when there was one) must
verify — otherwise `decrypt_error` (RFC 8446 §4.2.11 MUST; a binder of the wrong length counts
as wrong) — and nothing is decided before it, the binder of a ticket not taken is never looked
at; as in rustls the binder is checked before the PSK modes are, so a bad binder with only
`psk_ke` offered is still `decrypt_error`. The resumed handshake: ServerHello with `pre_shared_key` (the index) and a key share (a
fresh (EC)DHE always runs), early secret from the PSK, EncryptedExtensions without the SNI
acknowledgement (RFC 6066 §3), no Certificate or CertificateVerify, Finished; `isResumed()`.
Every buffer holding the resumption secret, the PSK or a ticket's plaintext is wiped before
the step returns. Not yet: a stateful cache, early data, the ticket count request (RFC 9149).

**Client certificates** (RFC 8446 §4.3.2, §4.4.2, §4.4.3; rustls 0.23 rules,
`Config.client_auth`). A full handshake sends a CertificateRequest after the
EncryptedExtensions: an empty context, `ClientAuth.schemes` as `signature_algorithms` (rustls's
list by default: ECDSA P-384/P-256, Ed25519, RSA-PSS, then RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 for the chain only),
the CA names of `ClientAuth.authorities` as `certificate_authorities` when there are any; a
resumption sends none. The client's Certificate (`clientauth.parseCertificate`, checked whole):
malformed is `decode_error`; another context `illegal_parameter`; an entry with any extension
`unsupported_extension` (the request asks for none). Empty: `certificate_required` when
`ClientAuth.mandatory` (the default), otherwise the client goes on unauthenticated (no
CertificateVerify). Otherwise: at most 16 certificates and a leaf of at most 4096 octets
(`bad_certificate` past either); the leaf's key must be one `certverify` verifies (RSA, ECDSA
P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, ML-DSA — the last two only with their schemes in
`ClientAuth.schemes`, and an ML-DSA-65/87 leaf is over the 4096-octet cap) and its `keyUsage`,
if present, must assert `digitalSignature`
(`unsupported_certificate`; BoringSSL checks this in the TLS layer whatever the verifier says,
read from an `x509.safe`-vetted copy); then the chain, leaf first, goes to
`ClientCertVerifier.verify` with the `ClientAuth.clock` time, whose refusal names the alert
(`bad_certificate`, `unsupported_certificate`, `certificate_revoked`, `certificate_expired`,
`unknown_ca`, `access_denied`, `certificate_unknown`). `X509Verifier` is RFC 5280 path
validation to the caller's anchors with the clientAuth extended key usage
(`x509.verifyChain`, rustls `WebPkiClientVerifier`); the leaf's names are the application's
business. The CertificateVerify over the transcript through the client's Certificate: a scheme
the server did not ask for, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (RFC 8446 §4.4.3) or one that does not suit the
leaf's key is `illegal_parameter`, a signature that does not verify `decrypt_error`. Then the
client's Finished as before. `peerCertificate()` is the leaf once its CertificateVerify verified
(never before), `peerSignatureScheme()` its scheme. Tickets carry both, so a resumption reports
the identity of the handshake that issued its ticket (rustls keeps the whole chain; here only
the leaf). With a mandatory certificate a ticket without one is not resumed (a full handshake
asks for the certificate; rustls resumes it). A ticket also carries when the certificate was
proved, carried across re-issued tickets: past the ticket lifetime from that full handshake the
ticket is not resumed, however young it is — so an expired or revoked certificate does not live
on through resumptions (rustls re-issues indefinitely). A failed handshake reports no identity.

**HelloRetryRequest** (RFC 8446 §4.1.4, rustls 0.23 rules): when the client sent no share for
the chosen group, the server fixes the suite, answers with a HelloRetryRequest naming the group
(no cookie) and a compatibility CCS, and restarts the transcript as
`message_hash(Hash(ClientHello1)) ‖ HelloRetryRequest` with the suite's hash (§4.4.1). The first
ClientHello must end its record flight (`unexpected_message`). The second must carry a share for
that group, the same SNI, still offer that suite, and no `early_data` — otherwise
`illegal_parameter`. Stricter than rustls, which re-chooses suite and group on the second hello
and compares only the hash: RFC 8446 §4.1.4/§4.2.8 bind both to the HelloRetryRequest
(independent review 2026-10-20, MEDIUM ×2); the ServerHello that follows has no second CCS.
Early data the first ClientHello announced is skipped in the clear up to 2^14 octets of
ciphertext, an empty record counting one octet (more: `unexpected_message`, as rustls). One compatibility CCS per ClientHello is
accepted (two in all).

**The blocking wrapper** (`connection.Connection`): the server over a `std.Io.Reader` /
`Writer`. Records are decrypted in place in the reader's own buffer (it must hold a whole
record), so `read` returns a slice of it, valid until the next read; pending output is flushed
before every wait, after the handshake, each `writeAll` and `close`; a refusal's alert is flushed
before the error is returned. A transport that ends before the handshake or mid-record is
`EndOfStream` (truncation).

RFC 8446 §5, record layer over a byte stream:

- **Header** (`parseHeader`, `writeHeader`): `ContentType type ‖ uint16 legacy_record_version ‖
  uint16 length`, 5 octets. Protected records carry `application_data` (23) and `0x0303`.
- **Protection** (`Protection.seal` / `open`), per direction: `TLSInnerPlaintext = content ‖
  ContentType type ‖ zeros[pad]`, sealed with the suite's AEAD under the traffic key; nonce =
  the 12-byte IV XOR the 64-bit sequence number left-padded to 12 octets (§5.3); additional
  data = the record header (§5.2). The sequence number starts at 0 for every key and advances
  by one per record. Opening strips the zero padding and takes the last non-zero octet as the
  content type (§5.4).
- **Keys** (`Protection.init`): key and IV from the traffic secret by HKDF-Expand-Label "key" /
  "iv" (§7.3, `tls13.keyschedule.tls13.deriveTrafficKeyIv`), hash and key length per suite:

  | Suite | Code | Hash | Key | AEAD |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 | 0x1301 | SHA-256 | 16 | `aesgcm.Aes128Gcm.Context` |
  | TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 | 0x1302 | SHA-384 | 32 | `aesgcm.Aes256Gcm.Context` |
  | TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 | 0x1303 | SHA-256 | 32 | `chachapoly.ChaCha20Poly1305` |

  The AES suites keep an expanded `aesgcm` context per direction, so a record pays no key
  schedule (the fork's per-direction context, which qap measured at 1.6–1.8× std at 16 KiB).
- **Receive side** (`inbound.Inbound.next`), sans-I/O: takes the received octets, returns one
  event — a whole handshake message, application data, `peer_closed` or `need_more` — and how
  many octets it is done with. Protected records are opened in place, so application data is a
  slice of the caller's buffer; handshake fragments are copied into a `Joiner` (caller's buffer,
  `Joiner.bufferLen(max_message)`, default cap 64 KiB as in rustls) which joins a message
  across records and splits several out of one. Rules (RFC 8446 §5; where it names no alert,
  rustls 0.23's choice):

  | Input | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Outer type not 20–23, version not `0x03XX`, empty non-`application_data` record | `decode_error` (header alone) |
  | Plaintext record > 2^14, protected > 2^14 + 256 | `record_overflow` (header alone) |
  | Handshake message over the joiner's cap | `decode_error` (its header alone) |
  | Another record type inside a fragmented handshake message | `unexpected_message` |
  | Receive key change with any handshake octet held (`installRx`) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext `change_cipher_spec` `0x01` after the first ClientHello, before the client Finished, ≤ 2 | dropped |
  | Any other CCS: before a ClientHello, after Finished, other content, a third one, protected | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext handshake or application data under a receive key; plaintext application data at all | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext alert under a receive key after a protected record was opened, or > 2 octets | `unexpected_message` |
  | Zero-length protected handshake or alert content (§5.4) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Application data before the engine sets `app_data_ok` (no 0-RTT) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Alert content not two octets | `decode_error` |
  | Alert of unknown level | `illegal_parameter` |
  | Warning other than `close_notify`, `user_canceled` | `decode_error` |
  | `user_canceled` warning | ignored, 4 per connection, then `unexpected_message` |
  | `close_notify` after the handshake / before it | `peer_closed` (later octets ignored) / abort, no alert |
  | Fatal alert | abort, no alert (`peer_alert` holds it) |

  `inbound.alertFor` maps each error to the alert to send (none for the peer's own abort).
- **ClientHello** (`hello.parseClientHello`, RFC 8446 §4.1.2): zero-copy into slices of the
  message; lists stay in wire form and are walked by iterators that cannot fail (every length was
  checked). Extensions read: `server_name`, `status_request`, `supported_groups`,
  `ec_point_formats` (checked, unused), `signature_algorithms`, `signature_algorithms_cert`, ALPN,
  `compress_certificate`, `session_ticket` (skipped), `pre_shared_key`, `early_data`,
  `supported_versions`, `cookie`, `psk_key_exchange_modes`, `certificate_authorities` (checked),
  `key_share`, `renegotiation_info` (checked); others are skipped. Strictness is rustls 0.23's:

  | Input | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Any length that does not add up, trailing octets in an extension or the message | `decode_error` |
  | `legacy_session_id` > 32, empty or odd `cipher_suites`, no compression method | `decode_error` |
  | An empty list RFC 8446 / 6066 / 7301 declare non-empty (groups, signature schemes, versions, ALPN, ALPN name, cookie, PSK modes, PSK identities/binders, point formats) | `decode_error` |
  | `early_data` with a body; an empty SNI `host_name` | `decode_error` |
  | Any extension type twice (known, unknown or GREASE); `pre_shared_key` not last; PSK identities and binders of different counts | `illegal_parameter` |
  | An empty `key_share` list | accepted (the client asks for a HelloRetryRequest) |
  | No extension block at all | accepted (the state machine refuses it: no `supported_versions`) |

  SNI: a valid DNS name (rustls-pki-types rules: 1–253 octets, labels 1–63 of letters, digits,
  `_`, `-` not at a label's ends, an optional trailing dot, last label not all digits) is
  `dns_name`; an IP literal is `ip_address` and treated as no SNI; anything else, a second
  `host_name` or an empty list is `invalid` (the state machine answers `illegal_parameter`). A
  name type other than `host_name` ends the list. `pre_shared_key.binders_offset` is where the
  binder transcript ends (§4.2.11.2). Duplicate detection is an 8 KiB bit set over the whole
  type space, so it is linear in the number of extensions.
- **Server messages** (`messages`, RFC 8446 §4): ServerHello, HelloRetryRequest (the §4.1.3
  random), EncryptedExtensions, Certificate (entries with their extensions, e.g. an OCSP
  `status_request` on the leaf, §4.4.2.1), CertificateVerify and Finished, each returned whole
  (header ‖ body) from the caller's buffer; ALPN and OCSP extension bodies. ServerHello extension
  order is `pre_shared_key`, `key_share`, `cookie`, `supported_versions` (RFC 8448's). A field
  too long for its length prefix is `FieldTooLong`, a short buffer `BufferTooSmall`.
- **In place:** `seal` takes the content at `buf[5..]` and writes type, padding, tag and header
  around it; `open` decrypts over the ciphertext and returns a slice of the same buffer. That is
  the layout qap's zero-copy record codecs read and write.

## Constant-time contract

**Key loading** (`keys`): the private key's PEM body is decoded by `b64ct` (constant time) into
a stack buffer that is wiped on every exit; the block search walks block by block and skips a
foreign body with a scan for its END line's first `-` (a compare false on every base64
character), never a Boyer-Moore-Horspool `std.mem.find` over key text — `acme`'s `pemBlockStart`
approach. The DER walk branches on tags and lengths (the key's layout, not its value); the
scalar range check and the key-to-leaf comparison are std's and a `mem.eql` over public values.
`fromPem` runs under a 64 KiB burn (`burn.key_burn`; unburned 35 / 39 / 31 KiB for P-256 /
P-384 / Ed25519, an RSA parse burns its own below), held by `src/stackprobe_test.zig`. No
ctgrind row yet.

Secrets: the traffic secret, the AEAD key state and the IV. The AEADs are the collection's
(`aesgcm` with its own ctgrind rows, `chachapoly`); the code here branches only on public
values — the suite, lengths, the sequence number, the tag verdict. The content-type scan in
`open` runs over the decrypted inner plaintext from its end and stops at the first non-zero
octet, so its time reveals the padding length; that is what rustls and OpenSSL do as well, and
the padding length is not a secret the record layer protects (padding hides the content length
from the wire, not from the receiver's timing). No ctgrind row yet (*Open*).

Dead stack (`CONVENTIONS.md` §2.1.1): secrets in by `*const`, key state held in the caller's
`Protection`, wiped by `Protection.wipe`. `init` / `initKeyIv` run under a 1 KiB burn (their
HKDF and AES key expansion burn their own 8 KiB below); `seal` / `open` under 4 KiB
(`burn.record_burn`; AES-GCM in place reaches 1.2–1.4 KiB, ChaCha20-Poly1305 burns its own).
Measured and held by `src/stackprobe_test.zig` (ReleaseFast).

The receive side branches only on framing values (record types, lengths, the handshake header,
the alert octets). Decrypted application data stays in the caller's buffer; joined handshake
messages stay in the joiner's buffer until `Inbound.wipe`, which zeroes every octet the joiner
ever wrote and the receive key.
The send side likewise: `Outbound.wipe` (from `Server.deinit`) zeroes the send key and every
octet of the output buffer written since `init` — up to its high-water mark (`Outbound.dirty`:
content framed or refused by `commit`, `write`, and what `touch` reports), not the whole
buffer. A `writeSlot` not yet committed counts in full; `abandonWrite(n)` (what
`Connection.deinit` calls) narrows it to the `n` octets written. An encoder that fails
(`OutputFull`, `InternalError`) marks the whole buffer. Every per-connection wipe of a buffer
uses `zeroize` (volatile 32-byte stores): `std.crypto.secureZero` stores a byte at a time, and
wiping qap's 48 KiB output that way cost ~16 µs a connection.

## Limits and refusals

The receive side's refusals are the table under *Wire format*. Record protection:

- `TLSInnerPlaintext` ≤ 2^14 + 1 octets (§5.2): `seal` refuses more (`RecordOverflow`), `open`
  refuses an authentic one that is larger (`RecordOverflow`, the `record_overflow` alert).
- `TLSCiphertext.length` ≤ 2^14 + 256 (§5.2): checked by `open` before any decryption
  (`RecordOverflow`). `max_record_len` (16,645) sizes a receive buffer for one whole record.
- A record shorter than a tag plus the type octet, or failing authentication: `BadRecordMac`
  (the `bad_record_mac` alert), with the ciphertext zeroed and the sequence number unchanged.
- A protected record whose outer type is not `application_data`: `UnexpectedRecordType`.
- An inner plaintext that is all zeros: `MissingContentType` (§5.4, `unexpected_message`).
- Sequence number 2^64 − 1: both directions refuse (`SequenceExhausted`); the engine must
  KeyUpdate first (§5.3). When to KeyUpdate earlier, at the AEAD's usage limit (§5.5), is the
  engine's policy: `Server` rekeys at `max_records_per_key` (2^23), qap's bound.
- Records sent carry at most `Config.max_fragment_len` octets of content (2^14 by default,
  clamped to [512, 2^14]: rustls `max_fragment_size`, BoringSSL `SSL_set_max_send_fragment`);
  `minOutputLen` counts the extra records a smaller size makes. Records received may be 2^14.
- The send side keeps `alert_reserve` (24 octets) of the output buffer for one alert, so a fatal
  alert or close_notify can be queued however full the application left it.
- `Server.write` never cuts a record short to fit behind output still pending: it takes
  nothing (`OutputFull`) until the caller sends what waits, so record boundaries follow the
  data. An output below `full_record_output_len` (2^14 + 256 + 5 + 24) cuts records to what it
  holds even when empty.
- ClientHello: a `legacy_version` below 0x0301 is `protocol_version` even beside 0x0304 in
  `supported_versions` (RFC 8446 §D.5, OpenSSL; rustls ignores it). A key_share entry for a
  group missing from `supported_groups` (§4.2.8, a MAY) or for an obsolete_RESERVED group
  (§4.2.7) is `illegal_parameter`; obsolete groups in `supported_groups` alone are served
  (JDK 11 lists sect* and secp256k1 beside TLS 1.3, BoGo `Server-JDK11-*`), which
  tlsfuzzer's `test-tls13-obsolete-curves` (OpenSSL only with `--relaxed`) counts against.
- A client Finished of the wrong length is `decrypt_error`, as a wrong one (BoringSSL, rustls,
  BoGo `TrailingMessageData-TLS13-ClientFinished-TLS`); OpenSSL and tlsfuzzer want
  `decode_error`.
- A client certificate chain: at most `clientauth.max_chain_len` (16) certificates, a leaf of at
  most `clientauth.max_leaf_len` (4096) octets (`bad_certificate`), the whole message within the
  joiner's cap (64 KiB by default, `decode_error`). `minOutputLen(config, key)` sizes the output
  for the first flight with a CertificateRequest and for the tickets with the longest leaf.

## Anchoring

- **External:** RFC 8448 §3 — all seven protected records of the simple 1-RTT handshake
  (server EncryptedExtensions…Finished, client Finished, NewSessionTicket, both application
  data records, both close_notify alerts) sealed byte-exact and opened back, under the RFC's
  keys, IVs and sequence numbers; and the RFC's server handshake traffic secret deriving the
  key and IV it printed. Extracted from the RFC text by `tools/rfc8448_records.py`, which
  re-opens every record with Python `cryptography` (OpenSSL) before writing
  `src/record_kat_vectors.zig`.
- **External (foreign implementation):** OpenSSL 3.5.5 `s_client` over loopback TCP
  (`tools/interop.zig`, `zig build interop-tlsserver`): twelve sessions — P-256 under OpenSSL's
  defaults (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, X25519MLKEM768), TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 over X25519,
  TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 over secp256r1, P-256 under SHA-384 over X25519, P-256 over
  secp384r1, a P-384 certificate (`ecdsa_secp384r1_sha384`) over secp384r1, an Ed25519 and
  an RSA-PSS certificate, ALPN `h2` chosen from `http/1.1,h2`, no SNI, and two
  HelloRetryRequests (s_client's lone X25519 share against a server with only secp256r1 under
  SHA-384, only secp384r1 under TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256), and two KeyUpdates (the server asks
  with `update_requested` before "pong", under SHA-384 and ChaCha20; s_client answers only
  with its next application data, so the tool hands it "again") — each verified by
  s_client against the test certificate and `localhost`, with ping/pong and close_notify.
  `--capture` records every octet both ways into `src/interop_vectors.zig`;
  `src/interop_replay_test.zig` drives a server with the same seed through `Connection` over
  OpenSSL's recorded octets and requires the recorded answer byte for byte (and refuses the
  recording with one octet flipped), in every test lane.
- **External (foreign implementation):** Go 1.26.8 crypto/tls client (`tools/go_client/main.go`,
  built by the same tool with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`), twelve more sessions in the same tool and the
  same capture: Go's defaults (X25519MLKEM768, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256), TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (the server enabling only that suite: Go's TLS 1.3 suite
  order cannot be configured), secp256r1 and secp384r1 as Go's only group, a P-384, an Ed25519
  and an RSA-PSS certificate, ALPN `h2`, no SNI (verified by hand in `VerifyConnection`), and a
  server without the hybrid taking Go's X25519 share without a retry, and two HelloRetryRequests
  (Go's two default shares against a server with only secp256r1, or only secp384r1 under
  TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384; Go's `ConnectionState.HelloRetryRequest` printed). The Go client verifies the
  chain with `x509.Certificate.Verify`, prints the negotiated version, suite, group (`CurveID`)
  and ALPN — anchored on the end of the line, so `X25519` does not match `X25519MLKEM768`
  (negative control 2026-10-20: the no-hybrid case against a server with the hybrid fails) —
  and requires close_notify (`io.ReadAll` without an error).
- **External (foreign implementation):** whole handshakes against Zig std's
  `crypto.tls.Client` (`src/handshake_test.zig`, in one thread through in-memory pipes): an
  ECDSA P-256 certificate (self-signed test fixture, `tools/test_certs.py`) verified by the
  client against SNI `localhost`, under TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and
  TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 with X25519MLKEM768, and under X25519 and secp256r1; a request,
  a response and close_notify each way (std's client advertises `ed25519` but cannot verify it,
  so Ed25519 and RSA are covered by the OpenSSL sessions). The same handshake with P-256 and
  P-384 chains and keys loaded by `keys` from the openssl-written vectors (SEC1 and PKCS#8).
  The same pipes with the collection's `tlsclient` (std's client with `x509.verifyChain`, grown
  to Go's client options): P-256, P-384, Ed25519 and RSA-PSS certificates verified; every group
  as the lone key share × every suite (12 handshakes); tlsclient's two default shares against a

  `ConnectionInfo` (suite, group, ALPN, peer chain) checked against the server's

  secp384r1 under each suite (6 handshakes, the client's `hello_retry_request` set).
- **External (foreign implementation):** `keys` on private keys in every PEM form the OpenSSL
  3.5.5 command line writes — `ecparam -genkey` (an `EC PARAMETERS` block, then SEC1), `ec`,

- **External (foreign implementation):** TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and

- **External:** RFC 8448's ClientHellos — §3 (1-RTT), §4 (resumed 0-RTT: `early_data`,
  `pre_shared_key` with one identity and binder), §5 (ClientHello1 and ClientHello2 with the

  prefix and its hash before writing `src/message_kat_vectors.zig`.

- **External:** the server's messages of RFC 8448 — §3 ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions,
  Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished; §4 ServerHello (with `pre_shared_key`) and
  EncryptedExtensions (with `early_data`); §5 HelloRetryRequest (with the cookie ClientHello2
  echoes) and the secp256r1 ServerHello; §6 CertificateRequest — rebuilt byte-exact from their
  fields by `messages` (same tool, `src/message_kat_vectors.zig`).

- **External:** RFC 8448 §6 (client authentication) end to end on the server's side: a server
  white-box at the client's second flight (the transcript through the RFC's server Finished)
  takes the RFC's client Certificate (RSA), verifies its CertificateVerify (RSA-PSS) and, under
  the RFC's client handshake traffic secret, its Finished — which covers the transcript through

- **External (foreign implementations):** client certificates from OpenSSL 3.5's `s_client`
  (`-cert`/`-key`: ECDSA P-256, RSA-2048 with RSA-PSS, Ed25519; an optional request answered
  with none; tickets after client authentication and their resumption) and Go 1.26's crypto/tls
  client (the same) against `X509Verifier` over a test client CA (`tools/client_certs.py`,
  `client_certs.zig`) — 11 more interop sessions (46 in all), captured and replayed byte-exact;
  the server must end with the presented leaf as `peerCertificate`, from the ticket on a

  `unsupported_certificate`, expired → `certificate_expired`, another CA → `unknown_ca`), a key

- **External (foreign test suite):** BoringSSL's BoGo runner (`ssl/test/runner` at 784fcafc,

  offered `rsa_pss_rsae_sha512`, which it cannot encode (`tls13.certverify.canSign`; signing
  then failed with `internal_error` instead of refusing with `handshake_failure`).

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

## Fuzzing

`src/fuzz_test.zig`, harness `tlsserver-record` (`TLSSERVER_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`,
testkit's deterministic driver; `zig build --fuzz` keeps working through a `ScriptSource`). For
a random suite and traffic secret a sealed record (content length 0..1200 with the short edge
weighted, inner type, padding) opens back to the same content and type; the same record damaged
— one flipped bit, a header octet rewritten, truncation or extension, random ciphertext — or
opened under another sequence number is refused, never accepted unless the bytes are
identical, never a panic, and a refused record never advances the sequence number.
`fuzz harness: record, 300 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Harness `tlsserver-inbound`: 1–4 handshake messages (bodies up to 20,000 octets) cut into records
at random points — short cuts, whole 2^14 records and anything between — plaintext or protected
under a random suite, with compatibility CCS records at message boundaries and, when protected,
application data and a close_notify after them, fed to `Inbound.next` in random chunk sizes
(1–8 octets one time in four). The events must give back exactly the messages, the application
data and the close; the same stream damaged (a flipped bit, a rewritten header octet,
truncation, spliced random octets) never panics, and damage that reaches a protected record
carrying output is never accepted with the genuine output. `fuzz harness: inbound, 300 seeds,
reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Verdict 2026-10-20: 8 × 1,500,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean (~42,000 runs/s per job). Five
planted mutants caught (schemata, one build): the sequence number left out of the nonce, the
header left out of the additional data, the sequence advanced on a failed open, the content
type kept in the content, the record-length check removed (a panic).

Verdict `tlsserver-inbound` 2026-10-20: 4 × 300,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean (~5,700 runs/s per
job). Five planted mutants caught: a whole message held back one octet, the joiner's compaction
left out, the last record left out of `consumed`, the header kept in the body, the protected
record limit set to the plaintext one (survived the first harness, which almost never cut a
whole 2^14 record; whole records are now one cut in eight).

Harness `tlsserver-hello`: a ClientHello built from a model — the fixed fields, a random subset
of nine known extensions with random well-formed bodies and up to three unknown ones, in random
order, `pre_shared_key` last one time in three — decodes to exactly the model (every list walked,
the SNI class, the binder offset); planted faults give their error (a repeated extension or
`pre_shared_key` not last: `illegal_parameter`; a 33-octet session id: `decode_error`). The same
message damaged never panics, and whatever it decodes to is walked to the end by every iterator
(bounds-checked in ReleaseSafe). Verdict 2026-10-20: 4 × 1,000,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean
(~23,800 runs/s per job). Six planted mutants caught: the duplicate check, the PSK-last check
and the 32-octet session id limit removed, the binder offset two octets early, the ALPN iterator
skipping one octet short (a panic), the key share read one octet early.

Harness `tlsserver-keys`: `keys.CertKeyPair.fromPem` on the key vectors — the key's DER with
octets rewritten (anywhere, or among the leading tags and lengths), truncated or extended and
re-armoured under its own or another key label; rebuilt from a model of its fields (version,
the scalar or seed at lengths around the curve's, own or other curve OIDs, optional `[0]` /
`[1]`, with or without the PKCS#8 wrapper, Ed25519 parameters that RFC 8410 forbids); or the
PEM text itself with octets rewritten or cut. Any outcome is a typed error, or exactly the
genuine key (compared with a genuine load); never a panic, never a leak. Verdict 2026-10-20:
4 × 30,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean (~450 runs/s per job, RSA dominates; rerun clean after
the review fixes below). Five planted mutants
caught: the DER length bound removed (a panic), the EC key-to-leaf comparison removed (a
different key loaded), the Ed25519 seed length check removed (survived the first harness,
which never shortened a nested octet string consistently — the model mode added), the scalar
length bound removed, the long-form length bound removed.

Harness `tlsserver-server`: `Server` as a whole, fed the recorded OpenSSL and Go client
streams (`interop_vectors.zig`) with the recorded seed, so its output is a function of its
input. The genuine stream cut into random chunks, or fed one octet at a time, ends exactly as
recorded; truncated, it never errs and its output is a prefix of the recording; a flipped bit
in a record body never ends as recorded and, up to the client's Finished, never completes the
handshake; a flipped header bit may be refused, stall (output a prefix) or pass (output exactly
the recording — the record version octets nobody reads); random octets spliced in at a record
boundary never panic. White box: the harness takes the client's handshake traffic secret from
the server, opens the client's Finished and reseals it — damaged (a verify_data bit, one octet
short, another message type) it is refused and the handshake never completes; intact with up
to 300 octets of padding it ends as recorded. Over every run: after a failure `feed` returns
`Closed`; the alert is the last record out — plaintext and exactly `alertFor`'s fatal alert if
the server had sent nothing else, else one sealed alert record, and none after the server's own
close_notify or for an error naming none; application data never precedes `handshake_done`;
`write` before it is `NotConnected`. RSA cases run one time in ten (signing dominates).
`fuzz harness: server, 400 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane. Verdict
2026-10-20: 4 × 40,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean (~1,070 runs/s per job). Five planted mutants
caught: the client's Finished check removed (survived the first harness — every change to the
ClientHello changes the client's keys, so damage never got past the AEAD to the Finished
check; the resealing white-box mode added), the failed state not kept, one octet more awaited
than a record needs, any change_cipher_spec body accepted, the alert after the flight left out.
The KeyUpdate recordings (2026-10-20) are driven with the same KeyUpdate before "pong" (and
s_client's "again"); 4 × 12,000 runs clean.

Harness `tlsserver-keyupdate`: `Server` after a recorded handshake (fed through the client's
Finished), then up to 24 scripted post-handshake steps against a model client that follows
every key: client KeyUpdates of either request, whole or split over two records; client
application data, empty records included; server writes, an output left full,
`Server.keyUpdate` either way, the send key set just short of `max_records_per_key` (white
box), close_notify; and one closing refusal — an invalid request octet, a wrong length, a
KeyUpdate sharing its record with the next message, more than `max_key_updates` in a row, a
record under the client's previous key. Invariants: every server record opens under the
model's keys, in order; data arrives intact both ways; a requested KeyUpdate is out before the
server's next application data; the number of server KeyUpdates, and of those requesting one
back, is exactly what the requests, the `keyUpdate` calls and the key limit account for
(coalesced while one stays queued, dropped after close_notify); a refusal is the predicted
error, its alert the last record, sealed under the key in force; nothing is accepted after.
`fuzz harness: keyupdate, 400 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane. Verdict
2026-10-20: 4 × 12,000 runs, ReleaseSafe, clean (~750 runs/s per job). Seven planted mutants
caught, each within seconds: the reply sealed under the new key, the KeyUpdate count not reset
by application data, `update_requested` never answered, no rekey at the limit, no alert
reserve (the harness's first run found that defect for real: a full output dropped the fatal
alert), an invalid request octet taken as `update_not_requested`, a deferred reply dropped.

Client certificates (2026-10-20). `tlsserver-server` and `tlsserver-keyupdate` replay the
mTLS recordings with the recorded `client_auth` (`X509Verifier` over the test client CA): the
keyupdate harness feeds the client's sealed records one at a time up to `handshake_done` (Go
sends Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished in records of their own, OpenSSL in one); the
server harness's white-box reseal takes the client's first sealed record, which now holds its
Certificate — damaged (a bit flipped anywhere in it, an octet short, a Finished where the
Certificate belongs) it is refused and the handshake never completes; repadded it ends as
recorded. Harness `tlsserver-clientauth`: a client Certificate message of zero to three real
certificates (the test client CA's leaves, the CA itself, an expired one, a P-384 server
certificate), whole — it decodes to the same chain, the leaf's key reads, the CA (keyCertSign
only) is refused for signing — or damaged (bit flips, an octet rewritten, truncation, splices),
when every certificate it still decodes to goes through `leafPublicKey` and `checkLeafKeyUsage`
(std's DER walk on an `x509.safe` copy) without a panic; then a CertificateVerify body, maybe
truncated. Verdicts 2026-10-20, ReleaseSafe, clean: `tlsserver-server` 4 × 60,000 (~1,150
runs/s per job), `tlsserver-keyupdate` 4 × 20,000, `tlsserver-clientauth` 4 × 1,500,000 (~35,000
runs/s per job). Eighteen planted mutants (schemata, one build, the whole test suite per
mutant) caught: the certificate's proof age not checked on resumption, an empty certificate let through when mandatory, the verifier skipped, an
unadvertised scheme or a bad signature accepted, the server's context string in the client's
signed content, a ticket without a certificate resumed under a mandatory one, tickets without
the certificate, `peerCertificate` before the CertificateVerify, a CertificateRequest on a
resumption, the resumed identity lost, entry extensions or another context accepted, an empty
`cert_data`, `digitalSignature` ignored, an expiry reported as `bad_certificate` — and two that
survived the first pass, now caught by new tests: the server not calling the key-usage check
(only `clientauth`'s own test covered it) and the ticket's leaf-length cap (the test's ticket
was too short to get there).

Independent read-only review of `keys` (Sonnet, 2026-10-20): no HIGH. MEDIUM fixed — an EC
scalar ≥ the order loaded and failed only at the first signature (std's `fromBytes` does not
range-check; test with d = n, n + 1, 0). LOWs fixed: legacy `Proc-Type` encrypted keys gave
`InvalidPem` (now `UnsupportedKey`); a skipped block with a cut END line swallowed the next
BEGIN (END must now match); one pass over the blocks instead of one per label; intermediates
are checked; the key's size limit no longer counts whitespace; an RSA-PSS leaf is named. Added:
an allocation-failure sweep (`checkAllAllocationFailures`) over every key form, CRLF, `out`
zeroed after an error. Documented, not changed: the pair must not move after `certifiedKey`,
and `fromPem` wants ~110 KiB of stack (more for RSA; for ML-DSA, 2026-10-21, up to 1.3 MiB —
`burn.mldsa_key_burn`). A handshake signs and exchanges under `tls13`'s burns: up to 352 KiB
for an ML-DSA-87 signature and 256 KiB for ML-KEM-1024 (ReleaseFast depths ×1.3; Debug frames
are larger), so a small-stack worker must be sized for the keys and groups it enables.

## What is deliberately not done

- **TLS 1.2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0/1.1:** never. The suites and the record format are TLS 1.3's only.
- **0-RTT early data:** not in v1 (qap refuses early data). Planned for M4 as opt-in with
  stateful single-use tickets and `tlsresume.replay`.
- **kTLS:** not in v1 — measured in qap at 41 % slower than userspace records; a secret-export
  hook may come with M4.
- **Strict parsing of extensions a TLS 1.3 server ignores** (`extended_master_secret`,
  certificate types, QUIC parameters, ECH): skipped as unknown, where rustls checks their form —
  a difference only in what malformed-but-ignored octets are refused.
- **Constant-time padding removal:** not done, as in rustls and OpenSSL (see the constant-time
  contract).
- **FFDHE groups, AES-CCM suites, brainpool and x448 / Ed448:** not offered (rustls's default
  provider neither); tlsfuzzer's scripts for them stay red by design (`tools/tlsfuzzer/baseline.tsv`).
- **psk_ke (PSK without (EC)DHE) and external PSKs:** never (rustls likewise).

## Backlog / deferred

- **M1 closed 2026-10-20:** secp384r1 and P-384 certificates; the key loader; interop with the
  Go client and `tlsclient`; the `tlsserver-server` fuzz harness; the BoGo shim (130 pass).
- **M4 step 1 (2026-10-21): ML-KEM-1024, P-521 and ML-DSA** — 16 of the 49 gaps closed (BoGo
  359/0, parity 267 of 436, 33 gaps). Open: ML-DSA-65/87 client leaves (5.5-7.5 KB) exceed
  `clientauth.max_leaf_len` — raising it costs every connection 4 KiB (`Server.peer_buf`) and
  ticket scratch; a caller-supplied leaf buffer (the qap item below) is the other way: an owner
  decision (`Server-Verify-ML-DSA-65/87`, `Server-InvalidSignature-ML-DSA-65/87` disabled with
  that reason). The ML-DSA AlgorithmIdentifier's absent parameters are checked for the private
  key, not for a client leaf (`x509.Spki` does not expose them).
- **rustls parity gaps (2026-10-20, 49 tests, `--bogo` prints them as `GAP`):** 0-RTT (27:
  `EarlyData-*`, `TLS13-MaxEarlyData-*`, `TLS13-TicketAgeSkew-*-60-*`, EndOfEarlyData) and
  certificate compression (6, RFC 8879) are M4; P-521 and ML-DSA server keys (12:
  `Server-Sign*-ECDSA_P521_SHA512`, `Server-Sign*-ML-DSA-*`; zig-libs has `p521` and an ML-DSA
  module would be needed in `tls13.certverify`) and standalone ML-KEM-1024 as a group (4,
  `CurveTest-*-MLKEM1024`, `tls13.kex`) are not scheduled yet. `-expect-session-id`
  (BoringSSL's stateful session cache) waits for the stateful cache (M4). The owed list is
  re-derived with `tools/bogo/rustls_parity.py` when the rustls reference moves (it takes
  about 4 minutes).
- **Second ClientHello unchanged (2026-10-21, tlsfuzzer `test-tls13-shuffled-extentions`, 17):**
  RFC 8446 §4.1.2 has the client resend the same ClientHello after a HelloRetryRequest but for
  the listed changes; only the suite, the group's share, SNI and early_data are compared now
  (rustls compares less). A comparison of the first hello's other extensions (kept as a hash
  of their octets) would refuse a reordered or altered one with `illegal_parameter`.
- **Key loading:** encrypted PKCS#8 (`rsa` already decrypts PBES2 for RSA keys:
  `fromPemEncrypted`), a private-key reader shared with `acme` (request filed in
  `x509/SPEC.md` § Backlog).
- **M2:** ~~HRR~~ (step 1, 2026-10-20), ~~KeyUpdate~~ (step 2, 2026-10-20), ~~NewSessionTicket and resumption through `tlsresume`~~ (step 3, 2026-10-20), ~~mTLS through
  `x509.verifyChain`~~ (step 4, 2026-10-20), ~~OCSP stapling~~ (step 5, 2026-10-20, with SCT
  lists). Later for stapling: a staple per selected certificate already works through
  `Config.certificate.select`; BoringSSL's server OCSP callback (`ServerOCSPCallback-*`, disabled
  by rustls too) and parsing the staple (expiry, matching the leaf) are not done — the caller
  refreshes it.
  `CertifiedKey.check` runs right after certificate selection, before the signature scheme is
  matched: a misconfigured key is `internal_error` even for a client that could not have used it
  (configuration errors first). After a HelloRetryRequest the second ClientHello's
  `status_request` / `signed_certificate_timestamp` decide (as in rustls; RFC 8446 §4.1.2 would
  have them unchanged — only the SNI is compared).
- **Client leaf cap as a Config field (qap, 2026-10-21):** `clientauth.max_leaf_len` (4096) is a
  constant, so is `Server.peer_buf`; qap's `Tls.max_client_cert_bytes` goes up to 16384 and its
  tlsserver path refuses a configuration above 4096 at compile time (`src/session.zig`
  `secureZl`). Ideal: the leaf buffer supplied by the caller (as `joiner_buf`), its length the cap.
- **Client certificates, later:** raw public keys (RFC 7250, rustls has them), the whole client
  chain kept for the application (rustls `peer_certificates`; here the leaf), P-521 and ML-DSA
  client keys (with `tls13.certverify`), post-handshake authentication (not in rustls either). **M3:** the differential run against the fork and
  qap on a branch; the seams are in (2026-10-21: one send buffer, `Connection.reader()`/`writer()`
  in place, `Server.writeSlot`/`commitWrite`; the fork's atomics are not needed — qap reads and
  writes a connection from one fiber, and the rekey bound is `max_records_per_key`, 2^23 as qap's);
  the curve arithmetic moved to `ct25519`/`p256`/`p384` on 2026-10-21 (through `tls13`).
  Server-side handshakes per second, replayed recordings (`TLSSERVER_BENCH`, ReleaseFast, one
  core, this host, best of 5 × 0.4 s): P-256 certificate + X25519 + TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 2,012
  → 6,705; X25519MLKEM768 1,825 → 4,788; P-384 certificate 506 → 1,832; Ed25519 3,036 → 3,491;
  RSA-2048 1,124 → 1,202; resumption 4,480 → 5,496. Not a P-axis number (that is the in-memory
  harness against OpenSSL libssl, M4).
  **M4:** rustls scope (0-RTT, certificate compression), ctgrind, mutation, independent review.

## Open

- KeyUpdate review 2026-10-20 (Sonnet, read-only): no HIGH or MEDIUM; four LOWs fixed the same
  day (see CHANGELOG). Accepted as rustls does: an empty application-data record resets the
  KeyUpdate count, so a peer may alternate 32 KeyUpdates and an empty record (one HKDF and two
  key setups per 27 octets it sends; replies stay bounded, one at a time). The KeyUpdate path
  holds only pointers in its own frames (HKDF and record setup burn their own) and is not yet
  in the stack probe.

- Client-certificate review 2026-10-20 (Sonnet, read-only): no HIGH. MEDIUM fixed: re-issued
  tickets kept a certificate alive indefinitely (now bounded by the lifetime from its proof).
  LOWs fixed: an unknown revocation status is `certificate_unknown` (rustls); the shim's
  lingering close is bounded in time; a failed handshake clears the identity; `ClientAuth.schemes`
  precondition documented. Accepted: the leaf's key and keyUsage are checked before the verifier
  (BoringSSL's order; rustls verifies first, so an untrusted unusable leaf gets
  `unsupported_certificate` here, `unknown_ca` there); a chain signature that does not verify is
  `bad_certificate` (rustls: `decrypt_error`); 4 KiB of `peer_buf` per `Server`.

- `burn.handshake_burn` (32 KiB around each handshake step since client certificates: the ticket
  plaintext and blob buffers hold a client leaf) is a margin, not a measured depth: the stack
  probe does not drive the server yet. The client Certificate and CertificateVerify steps run
  unburned: they touch no secret.
- `tlsserver-server` drives `Server` only through recorded clients (plus resealed Finished);
  a model client that builds ClientHellos from fields (as `tlsserver-hello` does) is not there.
- Independent read-only review 2026-10-20 (Sonnet, of server/inbound/outbound): no HIGH; the
  MEDIUM (KeyUpdate / AEAD limit) closed by M2 step 2; LOWs fixed the same day
  (`cipherSuite` before a suite was chosen, secrets kept after a failure, two compatibility CCS
  with one ClientHello, every kex error as `illegal_parameter`, an unknown enabled suite) or
  accepted: the 0-RTT skip budget of 2^14 octets cannot skip a full-size early record (rustls has
  the same budget).

- No ctgrind row and no audit or mutation run yet; the record layer is new code.
- The bulk path is not measured against OpenSSL libssl (P2), nor is the cost of the per-record
  4 KiB burn on small records.
